name: Hemp seed oil

lead: Hemp seed oil is pressed from the seeds of low-THC hemp plants and is high in linoleic and alpha-linolenic fatty acids. It appears in moisturisers, soaps and haircare, used by people who want soft, smooth, well-hydrated skin.

The chain is emollient: the fatty-rich oil sits on the skin surface, supports the barrier and seals in moisture. Proponents attribute benefits to its essential fatty acids, which is described mainly in product labelling and composition studies. Two small registered human studies of topical hemp oil products exist; results were not found. It is distinct from CBD extracts.

paras: Used as a face or body oil, or in creams, applied after cleansing or on damp skin to lock in moisture, and in hair products as a conditioning oil. It is often layered over a humectant such as hyaluronic acid or glycerin. Users generally notice softness right away.

Topical products carry standard external-use labelling. Analytical studies have measured trace cannabinoids in some commercial oils, carried over from plant material during processing. Patch testing is the usual precaution for sensitive skin.

angle.text: Hemp seed oil is used in moisturisers and body care by people wanting soft, well-hydrated skin. Its high linoleic acid content helps support the skin barrier and seal in moisture, leaving skin looking smoother.

lead: Hemp seed oil is a plant oil pressed from the seeds of low-THC varieties of Cannabis sativa. It is used as a food oil, in body-care products such as soaps, shampoos and moisturisers, and in industrial products such as paints and finishes.[1] It is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, chiefly linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.[2][1]

In skincare and haircare, it is marketed as a moisturising, nourishing ingredient. The sources available for this article are mostly chemical and food-science analyses of the oil rather than trials of its effect on skin or hair; two small registered human studies of topical hemp oil products are listed, and neither has published results in the material reviewed.[3][4]

Hemp seed oil is distinct from cannabidiol (CBD) extracts made from the flower and leaf. Seeds contain no cannabinoids themselves, but trace amounts can be carried onto the oil from plant material during processing, which is why analytical studies have measured cannabinoid content in commercial oils.[1][5][6]
infobox: Seeds of Cannabis sativa (low-THC hemp varieties)
Moisturisers, soaps, shampoos, tattoo aftercare creams[1][8]

paras: A phytochemical analysis of hemp seed oil found linoleic acid (about 55%), alpha-linolenic acid (about 16%) and oleic acid (about 11%) to be its most abundant fatty acids, along with a small unsaponifiable fraction.[2] Other descriptions also list gamma-linolenic and stearidonic acids in smaller amounts and an omega-6 to omega-3 ratio of roughly 3:1.[1]

Cold-pressed hemp seed oil has been reported to show antioxidant activity in laboratory assays, alongside other cold-pressed seed oils.[3] Formulation studies have examined how the oil behaves in emulsions of the kind used in cosmetic and pharmaceutical products.[7]

Refined hemp seed oil is used mainly in body-care products.[1] One US-listed topical product combining hemp seed oil is labelled as a tattoo-aftercare cream; its label describes it as relieving stinging, moisturising and supporting tattoo healing, and carries the warning 'for external use only'.[8] These are manufacturer label statements, not trial findings.

Analytical studies of commercial hemp seed oils have detected cannabinoids, including cannabidiolic acid, in some products, and have developed methods to quantify them so that levels of psychoactive cannabinoids can be assessed.[5][6] Researchers describe the composition as varying with the cultivar and the manufacturing method.[6] Canadian and EU authorities set differing limits for THC in hemp food products.[1]

No published trial of hemp seed oil for skin or hair appearance was identified. Registered studies include an early-phase case series of a topical hemp oil rich in cannabidiol and varin for androgenetic alopecia (NCT04842383, planned n=40, status unknown),[4] a completed trial of hulled hemp seed and oil in overweight adults (NCT02400203, n=30), which concerned diet rather than appearance,[9] and a skincare study for acne, eczema and skin ageing that was withdrawn before enrolment (NCT05873933).[10] No results from these registrations were available.
